name: ToolJet Cloud
tagline: Build and deploy a constrained internal data tool for a small team

pricing.notes: Public pricing is quote or usage dependent; canonical price is null.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: 2 builders; 50 end users; 2 apps; 100 AI credits/month

tiers.name: Pro
tiers.notes: $79/builder/month when billed annually; monthly price was not reliably exposed.

tiers.name: Team
tiers.limits: 100 end users; unlimited apps; 3,000 AI credits/builder/month; 14-day audit logs
tiers.notes: $199/builder/month when billed annually; monthly price was not reliably exposed.

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Custom builders, end users, apps, credits, support and deployment; starts at $3,000/month

pricing.freeTierCaps: 2 builders; 50 end users; 2 apps; 100 AI credits/month
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual (annual page advertises about 20% savings)
pricing.hiddenCosts: Pro/Team charge per builder and may require more seats as the maker team grows; extra AI capacity is $1 per 100 credits, and the Free plan cannot buy credit add-ons

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For ToolJet Cloud, build and deploy a constrained internal data tool for a small team. The hard boundary is connectors, runtime, permissions, enterprise controls, and hosted operations, plus connectors, runtime reliability, and governance.
coreLoopDIY: Define tables and views, build a constrained internal CRUD tool, connect one approved data source, and deploy it for a small trusted team.
requirements: API credentials for one selected integration
whatYouLose: connectors, runtime, permissions, enterprise controls, and hosted operations
ongoingBurden: schema migration, auth, permissions, connector drift, queues, deployments, backups, and auditability
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for ToolJet Cloud because the builder is only useful when its runtime, connectors, permissions, and deployments remain boring for years. The recurring cost buys schema migration, auth, permissions, connector drift, queues, deployments, backups, and auditability, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Appsmith
priorArt.desc: Large open-source low-code platform for internal applications and data sources.

alternatives.name: Appsmith Free
alternatives.desc: Five people can build and run database-backed internal apps in the hosted product without paying.

facts.install: Hosted signup for Appsmith Cloud Free
facts.engines: Appsmith's AI/agent features use Appsmith-managed AI services; exact model availability is product-controlled rather than a local backend
facts.dataFormat: App definitions, users, and secrets live in Appsmith Cloud; connected business data remains in the source database/API, while query results pass through Appsmith
facts.gapVsPaid: Appsmith Free is less generous for a tool with many end users and its hosted component and permission model differs enough to require rebuilding the app.

alternatives.name: Budibase
alternatives.desc: Internal apps, forms, automations, and portals in one box; much closer to Knack than its developer branding suggests.

facts.install: Docker image or Docker Compose; Kubernetes is also supported
facts.engines: Model-agnostic; the agent builder supports bring-your-own AI provider credentials
facts.dataFormat: Built-in app data and app definitions are stored in CouchDB, files in MinIO/S3-compatible object storage, and connected external data remains in its source system
facts.gapVsPaid: Budibase can replace the CRUD interface but gives up ToolJet Cloud's managed hosting and makes the user responsible for Docker, upgrades, backups, and availability.
facts.setupBlocker: Requires Docker and persistent storage; production use also means owning upgrades, TLS, backups, and database/network access

alternatives.name: Lowcoder
alternatives.desc: A self-hosted internal-tool canvas with a broad widget set; less polished, but not a toy.

facts.install: Single Docker image for evaluation, or Docker Compose/Helm with separate MongoDB and Redis services for production
facts.engines: Connectors include OpenAI and other APIs; the operator supplies provider credentials
facts.dataFormat: Users, app definitions, data-source configuration, and assets live in the deployment's MongoDB and mounted lowcoder-stacks volume; Redis holds sessions/state; external business data stays in its source
facts.gapVsPaid: Lowcoder is capable but noticeably less polished and documented, and self-hosting shifts all production operations away from ToolJet Cloud.
facts.setupBlocker: Docker is required; a production deployment needs MongoDB, Redis, secrets, backups, TLS, and more care than the all-in-one demo image

alternatives.name: Retool Free
alternatives.desc: The paid app's real builder, database, mobile apps, and 500 workflow runs for up to five people at $0.

facts.engines: Retool-managed AI models and agents; Free includes pooled AI credits and limited agent hours, while bring-your-own model keys are plan-dependent
facts.dataFormat: App definitions, Retool Database rows, and Retool file storage live in Retool Cloud; connected source data remains in the user's databases/APIs, although query results transit Retool
facts.gapVsPaid: Retool Free's tiny team allowance makes it unsuitable for the many-viewer internal tools that ToolJet's free and paid plans are designed to serve.

alternatives.name: ToolJet Free
alternatives.desc: The same cloud product is free for two builders, 50 end users, two apps, five database tables, and unlimited external data sources.

facts.install: Hosted signup for ToolJet Cloud Free
facts.engines: ToolJet AI uses vendor-hosted AI services and plan credits; bring-your-own LLM keys are an Enterprise add-on
facts.dataFormat: App metadata, ToolJet Database tables, secrets, and files live in ToolJet Cloud; connected source records remain in their external database/API
facts.gapVsPaid: It is the same service with caps on builders, apps, database tables, AI, and advanced governance, so a paid deployment may not fit without redesign.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Business plan and a small-team internal app DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for ToolJet Cloud in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, and Docker Compose; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: define tables and views, build a constrained internal CRUD tool, connect one approved data source, and deploy it for a small trusted team.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create a schema editor for text, number, boolean, date, enum, and relation fields.
Generate list, detail, create, edit, and kanban views from the schema.
Implement role-based read and write rules for admin and member roles.
Support one REST connector with encrypted credentials and explicit field mapping.
Add an activity log, CSV import or export, backups, and health checks.
Ship Docker Compose with migrations and a seeded example workspace.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out arbitrary user-authored code execution.
Deliberately leave out a broad integration marketplace.
Deliberately leave out native mobile binaries and enterprise compliance.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
